title: Single image to enterable world in seconds
author: Decent_Cell_3147
selftext:
Hi!

This is my very first post here. Typical vibe-coder story: I wanted to build something small, fell down a rabbit hole, and somehow ended up here. I think it's finally time to show a tiny glimpse of this funny little project I've been working on for the last few weeks.

It takes a single image of your choice, does a little bit of math, and a few seconds later you can start moving into the scene.

Everything happens locally in the browser and can run completely offline. AI isn't required at any stage; optional AI-assisted features are something I'm experimenting with separately.

There are no actual 3D models involved, and I'm not shipping scene geometry or texture assets alongside the source image. The scene in this clip is reconstructed at runtime using things like point clouds, depth/height information, normals, displacement, raymarching and a fair amount of math.

On my Xiaomi 14T Pro, this particular scene takes about 2.4 seconds to build.

The video itself contains only about 2.8 seconds of actual camera movement, slowed down to 10 seconds so the spatial stability is easier to see after video compression — especially the foliage, flowers and other tiny details.

That's basically all I'm trying to demonstrate here:

one flat image → click → a small space you can enter and navigate.

No Gaussian splatting, no generated GLBs, no Tripo-style reconstruction pipeline.

I'm curious what you think: is this worth pushing further?

I'm currently struggling with two related problems. First, I haven't found a convincing way to construct a procedural sky/background from the information I already have — height, normals, bump/displacement maps, point-cloud data, etc. The difficult part isn't producing a background, but making it feel like it exists at a believable distance from the reconstructed foreground.

That causes the second problem: I want to procedurally place trees and vegetation as natural scene boundaries, hiding areas where the original image simply contains no information. Without a reliable idea of where that distant boundary actually belongs, the vegetation tends to appear in plausible-looking but spatially wrong places.

Ideally, I'd like the reconstructed world to transition naturally into a distant tree line or similar boundary without visibly cutting through known geometry. If anyone has experimented with something similar, I'd love to hear how you'd approach it.

I'm also working on reconstructing missing building geometry by reusing what the image already tells me — duplicating or mirroring sufficiently visible faces where appropriate, keeping that inferred geometry separate from the known parts, and iterating from there.

I'm really happy with how far this little experiment has come, but I'd genuinely love some criticism, ideas or pointers.

There's quite a bit more hiding underneath this clip, so if people are interested I'd love to show more later.

comments.author: Decent_Cell_3147
comments.body:
I really appreciate the comments, but before I reply to every skeptic individually: What do you want to see? A predefined camera path? Multi-view shots? Complete frame-by-frame traceability?
Tbh - Your doubts are flattering. 😄
So: What exactly would kill those doubts? I won't make it open source yet, but I've got nothing to hide if that eleminates your concerns.
I told you what it's still lacking. I'm on it, it's kinda working, but still requires an rtx for proper use of Depthanything3. But it IS navigateable.

In the meantime, you might want to take a look at [Pants fishing - Monkey Island Forest](https://pants.fishing/mi1/forest/), because of the way the forest path is designed, discovered by some genius (obviously not me). my tool should be able to make the whole path visible, walkable, zoomable, turnable, tiltable, traceable in full 3D in no time as soon as I get those original (or remastered) assets (need all of them though).
